## Review: Supremum and Infimum

For a full treatment see [[supremum-infimum]]. We work in the extended reals
$\overline{\mathbb{R}}=\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}$, where every subset has a
supremum and an infimum.

:::{.definition data-title="Supremum & Infimum"}

Let $A\subseteq\overline{\mathbb{R}}$. The **supremum** $\sup A$ is the least
upper bound of $A$ and the **infimum** $\inf A$ is the greatest lower bound of
$A$. Equivalently, $s=\sup A$ if and only if $a\leq s$ for all $a\in A$ and, for
every $\epsilon>0$ (when $s<\infty$), there is $a\in A$ with $a>s-\epsilon$.

:::

The supremum and infimum need not be attained, unlike the max and min. For
example $\sup(0,1)=1\notin(0,1)$. Also $\inf A\leq\sup A$ for nonempty $A$, and
$A\subseteq B\implies\sup A\leq\sup B$ and $\inf A\geq\inf B$.

## Limit Supremum & Infimum of a Sequence

Let $\{x_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\overline{\mathbb{R}}$. The sequence of
**tail suprema** $s_n:=\sup_{m\geq n}x_m$ is decreasing, since we take the
supremum over fewer terms as $n$ grows. Dually the **tail infima**
$i_n:=\inf_{m\geq n}x_m$ are increasing. Monotone sequences in
$\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ always have a limit, which motivates the following.

:::{.definition data-title="Limsup & Liminf of a Sequence"}

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{m\geq n}x_m=\inf_{n\geq1}\sup_{m\geq n}x_m,
\qquad
\liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{m\geq n}x_m=\sup_{n\geq1}\inf_{m\geq n}x_m.
$$

:::

Both always exist in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ (even when $\lim x_n$ does not).
For example, $x_n=(-1)^n$ has $\limsup x_n=1$ and $\liminf x_n=-1$.

## Limit Supremum & Infimum of a Sequence of Sets

Order subsets of $X$ by inclusion. A least upper bound of $\{A_n\}$ is the
smallest set containing every $A_n$, and a greatest lower bound is the largest
set contained in every $A_n$. Hence
$$
\sup_{n\geq1}A_n=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n,\qquad\inf_{n\geq1}A_n=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n.
$$
Mimicking the definition for sequences, the tail supremum
$B_n=\bigcup_{m\geq n}A_m$ is decreasing and the tail infimum
$C_n=\bigcap_{m\geq n}A_m$ is increasing. A decreasing sequence of sets
converges to its intersection and an increasing sequence to its union.

:::{.definition data-title="Limsup & Liminf of a Sequence of Sets"}

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_n:=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty\bigcup_{m=n}^\infty A_m,
\qquad
\liminf_{n\to\infty}A_n:=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty\bigcap_{m=n}^\infty A_m.
$$

:::

The two definitions are the same under the dictionary
$\sup\leftrightarrow\cup$, $\inf\leftrightarrow\cap$, $\leq\leftrightarrow\subseteq$.
This is made precise by indicator functions.

:::{.proposition data-title="Indicator Functions"}

$\mathbf{1}_{\limsup A_n}=\limsup\mathbf{1}_{A_n}$ and
$\mathbf{1}_{\liminf A_n}=\liminf\mathbf{1}_{A_n}$ pointwise.

:::

The proof follows from the characterisations in the next section: $\mathbf{1}_{A_n}(x)\in\{0,1\}$,
so its limsup is $1$ exactly when it equals $1$ infinitely often.

## Equivalent Ways to Think About Limsup & Liminf

### Sets: "infinitely often" and "eventually"

:::{.theorem data-title="Limsup & Liminf of Sets"}

$$
\begin{align}
\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_n&=\{x: x\in A_n\text{ for infinitely many }n\}=\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\},\\
\liminf_{n\to\infty}A_n&=\{x: x\in A_n\text{ for all but finitely many }n\}=\{A_n\text{ eventually}\}.
\end{align}
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
$x\in\limsup A_n$ iff for every $n$ there is $m\geq n$ with $x\in A_m$, iff
$\{m: x\in A_m\}$ is unbounded, iff it is infinite. Also $x\in\liminf A_n$ iff
there is $n$ with $x\in A_m$ for all $m\geq n$, iff $\{m: x\notin A_m\}$ is
bounded, iff it is finite.
:::

So $\limsup$ is the set of points that keep returning to the sets, whereas
$\liminf$ is the set of points that eventually stay in the sets forever. In
probability, $\limsup A_n$ is the event "$A_n$ occurs infinitely often" and
$\liminf A_n$ is "$A_n$ occurs eventually", the starting point for the
[[borel-cantelli-lemma]].

### Sequences: "frequently" and "eventually"

:::{.theorem data-title="Characterisation of Limsup & Liminf"}

Let $L\in\overline{\mathbb{R}}$. Then $L=\limsup x_n$ if and only if

1. for every $a>L$, $x_n<a$ for all but finitely many $n$ (eventually), and
2. for every $a<L$, $x_n>a$ for infinitely many $n$ (frequently).

Dually, $\ell=\liminf x_n$ if and only if for every $a<\ell$, $x_n>a$
eventually, and for every $a>\ell$, $x_n<a$ infinitely often.

:::

:::{.proof}
($\Rightarrow$) If $a>L=\inf_ns_n$ there is $N$ with $s_N<a$, so $x_m<a$ for all
$m\geq N$. If $a<L$ then $s_n\geq L>a$ for every $n$, so for every $n$ there is
$m\geq n$ with $x_m>a$, hence $x_m>a$ for infinitely many $m$.

($\Leftarrow$) Assume 1 and 2. If $a>L$, 1 gives $s_n\leq a$ eventually, so
$\limsup x_n\leq a$, hence $\limsup x_n\leq L$. If $a<L$, 2 gives $s_n\geq a$ for
all $n$, so $\limsup x_n\geq a$, hence $\limsup x_n\geq L$.

The liminf statement follows by applying this to $-x_n$ using the duality below.
:::

### Sequences: subsequential limits

:::{.theorem data-title="Limsup as the Largest Subsequential Limit"}

$\limsup x_n$ is the largest and $\liminf x_n$ the smallest limit (in
$\overline{\mathbb{R}}$) of a subsequence of $\{x_n\}$.

:::

:::{.proof}
If $x_{n_k}\to\ell$ then $x_{n_k}\leq s_{n_k}$ and $s_{n_k}\to\limsup x_n$, so
$\ell\leq\limsup x_n$. Conversely, for $L=\limsup x_n$ finite, characterisation
2 with $a=L-1/k$, together with characterisation 1 with $a=L+1/k$, lets us
choose $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ with $L-1/k<x_{n_k}<L+1/k$, so $x_{n_k}\to L$. The cases
$L=\pm\infty$ are similar. The liminf is analogous.
:::

### Summary

| | $\limsup$ | $\liminf$ |
|---|---|---|
| Sequences | $\inf_n\sup_{m\geq n}x_m$ | $\sup_n\inf_{m\geq n}x_m$ |
| Sets | $\bigcap_n\bigcup_{m\geq n}A_m$ | $\bigcup_n\bigcap_{m\geq n}A_m$ |
| Meaning | frequently / infinitely often | eventually / all but finitely many |
| Subsequences | largest limit point | smallest limit point |

## Basic Inequalities and Identities

### For sequences

:::{.theorem data-title="Liminf $\leq$ Limsup"}

$\liminf x_n\leq\limsup x_n$.

:::

:::{.proof}
For every $n$, $i_n=\inf_{m\geq n}x_m\leq x_n\leq\sup_{m\geq n}x_m=s_n$. Hence
$i_n\leq s_n$, and taking $n\to\infty$ gives the claim.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Convergence"}

$\{x_n\}$ converges in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ if and only if
$\liminf x_n=\limsup x_n$, in which case
$\lim x_n=\liminf x_n=\limsup x_n$.

:::

:::{.proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Let $x_n\to x$. For finite $x$ and $\epsilon>0$ we have
$x-\epsilon<x_n<x+\epsilon$ eventually, so $x-\epsilon\leq i_n\leq s_n\leq x+\epsilon$
eventually. Hence $x-\epsilon\leq\liminf x_n\leq\limsup x_n\leq x+\epsilon$, and
$\epsilon\to0$ gives equality. If $x=+\infty$, then for every $M$ we have $x_n>M$
eventually, so $\liminf x_n\geq M$ for all $M$, hence
$\liminf x_n=\limsup x_n=+\infty$ (similarly for $-\infty$).

($\Leftarrow$) Let $L=\liminf x_n=\limsup x_n$ and take $a<L<b$ in
$\overline{\mathbb{R}}$. By the characterisation theorem, $x_n<b$ eventually
(applied to the limsup) and $x_n>a$ eventually (applied to the liminf). So
$x_n\in(a,b)$ eventually, which is the definition of $x_n\to L$ in the topology
of $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Duality, Monotonicity, Sums"}

For sequences in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$:

1. $\limsup(-x_n)=-\liminf x_n$.
2. If $x_n\leq y_n$ for all $n$, then $\limsup x_n\leq\limsup y_n$ and
   $\liminf x_n\leq\liminf y_n$.
3. $\limsup(x_n+y_n)\leq\limsup x_n+\limsup y_n$ and
   $\liminf(x_n+y_n)\geq\liminf x_n+\liminf y_n$, whenever the right-hand sides
   are defined (no $\infty-\infty$).

:::

:::{.proof}
(1) $\sup_{m\geq n}(-x_m)=-\inf_{m\geq n}x_m$; take the limit. (2) Each tail
supremum (resp. infimum) is monotone in the sequence, so pass to the limit. (3)
For $m\geq n$, $x_m+y_m\leq\sup_{k\geq n}x_k+\sup_{k\geq n}y_k$, so
$\sup_{m\geq n}(x_m+y_m)\leq s_n^x+s_n^y$; let $n\to\infty$. The liminf statement
follows from (1) applied to the first.
:::

> *Note:* The inequality in (3) can be strict, e.g. $x_n=(-1)^n$,
$y_n=-(-1)^n$ gives $x_n+y_n=0$ but $\limsup x_n+\limsup y_n=2$. If $x_n$
converges then equality holds.

### For sets

:::{.theorem data-title="Properties for Sets"}

1. $\liminf A_n\subseteq\limsup A_n$.
2. **Duality:** $(\limsup A_n)^c=\liminf A_n^c$ and
   $(\liminf A_n)^c=\limsup A_n^c$.
3. $\limsup(A_n\cup B_n)=\limsup A_n\cup\limsup B_n$ and
   $\liminf(A_n\cap B_n)=\liminf A_n\cap\liminf B_n$.
4. If $A_n\uparrow A$ or $A_n\downarrow A$ then $\lim A_n$ exists and equals
   $A$, i.e. $\liminf A_n=\limsup A_n=A$.

:::

:::{.proof}
(1) A point in all but finitely many $A_n$ is in infinitely many $A_n$. (2) By
[[set-theory-fundamentals#Algebra of Sets|De Morgan's laws]], $\left(\bigcap_n\bigcup_{m\geq n}A_m\right)^c=\bigcup_n\bigcap_{m\geq n}A_m^c$,
and similarly for the second. (3) $x\in A_n\cup B_n$ for infinitely many $n$ iff
$x\in A_n$ infinitely often or $x\in B_n$ infinitely often, as an infinite subset
of $\mathbb{N}$ covered by two sets has an infinite part in one of them. Likewise
$x$ is in both $A_n$ and $B_n$ for all but finitely many $n$ iff the exceptional
indices for $A_n$ and $B_n$ are each finite, since a union of two finite sets is
finite. (4) If $A_n\uparrow A$ then $\bigcap_{m\geq n}A_m=A_n$, so
$\liminf A_n=\bigcup_nA_n=A$, and $\bigcup_{m\geq n}A_m=A$ for all $n$, so
$\limsup A_n=A$. The decreasing case is dual.
:::
